# Results — Study 936 (Tolerance Bands) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One book, four schedules:
**drift** (never trade), **annual** (first session of each calendar year), **quarterly**
(first session of each quarter) and **5/25 bands** (trade whenever a sleeve is off target
by more than `min(5 percentage points absolute, 25% relative)`). Every schedule holds the
identical sleeves in the identical target mix, so this is a friction-and-timing contest,
not a forecasting contest. Signal read at the close of day t, traded at the close of day
t+1 (one execution lag). Cost is **one-way bps x traded notional / NAV**; nothing is
shorted, so there is no borrow leg. Sharpes are **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL's total
return). Daily total-return closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`). As-of **2026-06-30**
(the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint (returns) | Fingerprint (levels) |
|---|---|--:|---|---|
| SPY, IEF, GLD, BIL | 2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30 | 4,802 | **`958f652ce4c9`** | `aa48518ec578` |
| SPY, IEF (long cross-check) | 2003-01-03 → 2026-06-30 | 5,909 | **`7788344e5927`** | `7544783fda57` |

**The returns fingerprint is the reproducibility key.** `auto_adjust=True` closes carry a
cumulative dividend factor, so every new distribution rescales the entire historical *level*
series by a constant: the levels fingerprint moves on each refetch while not one return —
and therefore not one number in this file — has changed. Both are printed so a mismatch can
be diagnosed rather than merely noticed. (This is not hypothetical: the shared `_cache` SPY
parquet was refetched by a sibling study during the build, which moved the levels stamp and
left every statistic below bit-identical.)

BIL's 2007 inception gates the headline window: the excess-of-cash race wants a *tradable*
cash leg, not a synthetic bill rate.

## Book A — 60/40 SPY/IEF, excess-of-cash, 5 bps one-way

| Schedule | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max DD (abs) | Traded/yr | Rebalances | Cost drag |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| drift (never) | **+0.679** | +7.23% | 11.22% | −24.9% | 0.000 | 0 | 0.0 bp/yr |
| **annual** | **+0.667** | +6.79% | 10.71% | −30.0% | 0.079 | 19 | 0.4 bp/yr |
| **quarterly** | **+0.657** | +6.84% | 11.00% | −31.7% | 0.157 | 76 | 0.8 bp/yr |
| **5/25 bands** | **+0.641** | +6.88% | 11.40% | −31.9% | 0.114 | 22 | 0.6 bp/yr |

| Comparison | Sharpe diff | HAC *t* on the daily return difference | CAGR diff |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| bands − annual | **−0.026** | **+0.82** | +0.09 pp |
| bands − quarterly | −0.016 | +0.64 | +0.04 pp |
| quarterly − annual | −0.010 | +0.53 | +0.05 pp |

Note the split sign: the band book earns a *fractionally higher* mean daily return
(+0.06 bp/day, hence the positive *t*) and carries *more* volatility (11.40% vs 10.71%),
so its Sharpe comes out fractionally lower. Neither reading is anywhere near |*t*| = 2 —
the two effects are both noise, and they happen to point in opposite directions.

## Book B — 50/30/20 SPY/IEF/GLD, excess-of-cash, 5 bps one-way

| Schedule | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max DD (abs) | Traded/yr | Rebalances |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| drift (never) | +0.739 | +7.53% | 10.57% | −22.5% | 0.000 | 0 |
| **annual** | **+0.772** | +7.48% | 9.99% | −24.7% | 0.089 | 19 |
| **quarterly** | +0.756 | +7.48% | 10.23% | −26.4% | 0.172 | 76 |
| **5/25 bands** | +0.744 | +7.60% | 10.60% | −27.2% | 0.125 | 23 |

bands − annual: Sharpe **−0.028**, HAC *t* = **+0.80**. Adding a third, low-correlation
sleeve — the case where the 5/25 rule's *relative* leg finally bites (the 20% gold sleeve
gets a 2.5 pp band, not a 5 pp one) — changes nothing.

## Block-bootstrap CIs on the Sharpe **difference** (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks, paired)

| Book | Comparison | Point | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 60/40 | bands − annual | −0.026 | **[−0.067, +0.014]** | 87.9% |
| 60/40 | bands − quarterly | −0.016 | [−0.041, +0.010] | 87.2% |
| 60/40 | quarterly − annual | −0.010 | [−0.041, +0.021] | 71.3% |
| 50/30/20 | bands − annual | −0.028 | [−0.069, +0.015] | 88.6% |
| 50/30/20 | bands − quarterly | −0.012 | [−0.039, +0.016] | 78.4% |
| 50/30/20 | quarterly − annual | −0.016 | [−0.049, +0.019] | 79.6% |

Every interval straddles zero, and every one is narrow: this is not an underpowered test
that failed to see a large effect — it is a precise measurement of an effect that is
about **0.02 of a Sharpe point**, in the wrong direction for the claim.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2016-01-01), 60/40

| Era | n | annual | quarterly | bands | drift | bands − annual (*t*) | traded/yr bands vs annual |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007-05 → 2015-12 | 2,164 | +0.584 | +0.555 | +0.535 | +0.584 | **−0.049** (*t* = +0.15) | 0.127 vs 0.090 |
| 2016-01 → 2026-06 | 2,637 | +0.741 | +0.751 | +0.724 | +0.748 | **−0.017** (*t* = +0.83) | 0.081 vs 0.068 |

Same sign, same non-significance in both halves — including across the 2022 regime break
that flipped the stock/bond correlation, which is the single largest driver of how far a
60/40 book drifts.

## Cost sensitivity — costs are not the binding constraint

| One-way cost | annual | quarterly | bands | bands − annual (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.6677 | +0.6577 | +0.6416 | −0.026 (*t* = +0.83) |
| 5 bps | +0.6673 | +0.6570 | +0.6412 | −0.026 (*t* = +0.82) |
| 25 bps | +0.6658 | +0.6541 | +0.6392 | −0.027 (*t* = +0.78) |
| 50 bps | +0.6640 | +0.6505 | +0.6367 | −0.027 (*t* = +0.73) |

A 60/40 ETF book trades **7–17% of NAV a year** under every schedule tested. Even a
punitive 50 bps one-way — ten times a realistic SPY/IEF spread — costs the quarterly book
**7.9 bp/yr** and the band book **5.7 bp/yr**. The whole "bands save you turnover"
argument is worth single-digit basis points a year: it is real, and it is negligible.

## Band width is an ASSUMPTION — sweep it (60/40)

| Band | Excess Sharpe | Rebalances | Traded/yr | vs annual (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2% / 10% | +0.635 | 98 | 0.221 | −0.033 (*t* = +0.38) |
| 3% / 15% | +0.633 | 44 | 0.146 | −0.034 (*t* = +0.31) |
| **5% / 25%** | **+0.641** | **22** | **0.114** | **−0.026** (*t* = +0.82) |
| 8% / 40% | +0.654 | 9 | 0.076 | −0.013 (*t* = +0.93) |
| 10% / 50% | +0.649 | 6 | 0.063 | −0.019 (*t* = +1.42) |

The band width moves the Sharpe by 0.02 across a five-fold range of trigger widths, with
no monotone pattern beyond "trade less, keep a hair more". 5/25 is neither optimal nor
harmful — it is inside the flat region, which is the honest description of the whole
parameter.

## What the schedule *does* buy — weight discipline (60/40)

| Schedule | SPY weight min | max | final | mean abs deviation from 60% |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| drift | 0.357 | 0.850 | **0.846** | 0.102 |
| annual | 0.418 | 0.672 | 0.619 | 0.022 |
| quarterly | 0.481 | 0.666 | 0.628 | 0.013 |
| bands | 0.536 | 0.652 | 0.635 | 0.018 |

This is the one axis where the schedules genuinely differ and the band rule genuinely
wins: it delivers the **tightest weight envelope** (SPY never left 53.6–65.2%) for **27%
less traded notional than quarterly**. A do-nothing 60/40 book ended the sample at
**84.6% equity** — a completely different portfolio from the one it started as. That is a
risk-control result, not a return result.

Two honest qualifications on that win, since it is the only positive finding here:

1. **Bands are not the cheapest schedule** — annual is (0.079 traded/yr vs the band rule's
   0.114). Bands are the cheapest schedule *that holds a tight envelope*; annual buys its
   lower turnover with a 41.8–67.2% equity range, nearly twice as wide.
2. **Bands do not track target most closely on average** — quarterly does (mean absolute
   deviation 0.0133 vs 0.0178). What the band rule minimises is the *worst* excursion, which
   is the quantity a risk mandate is actually written on. Say which statistic you mean.

## Longer-window cross-check — SPY/IEF 2003-2026, **gross of cash**

BIL does not exist before 2007, so this window has no *tradable* cash leg and is run
gross-of-cash. Care is needed here, and the first draft of this study got it wrong:

- The cash leg cancels **exactly** in the daily return *difference*, so the HAC *t* is
  identical whether or not cash is subtracted (verified: +0.817 either way on the headline
  window).
- A Sharpe **ratio** is nonlinear, so the Sharpe *difference* is **not** cash-invariant —
  subtracting cash lowers both numerators and changes both denominators.

So the 23-year gross number may only be compared with a gross number. `verify.py` prints the
like-for-like conversion on the headline window:

| Comparison (2007-2026, 60/40) | Excess-of-cash | Gross-of-cash | HAC *t* (identical) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| bands − annual | −0.0261 | **−0.0340** | +0.82 |
| bands − quarterly | −0.0158 | −0.0204 | +0.64 |
| quarterly − annual | −0.0103 | −0.0136 | +0.53 |

| Schedule | Sharpe (gross-of-cash) | CAGR | Traded/yr | Rebalances |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| drift | +0.812 | +9.52% | 0.000 | 0 |
| annual | **+0.868** | +8.62% | 0.069 | 23 |
| quarterly | +0.856 | +8.68% | 0.143 | 93 |
| bands | +0.836 | +8.74% | 0.101 | 24 |

bands − annual over 2003-2026: **−0.032** gross-of-cash (HAC *t* = **+1.04**) — against the
**−0.034** gross-of-cash comparator on the 2007-2026 headline window. Twenty-three years,
same answer, now on the same basis. (Read naively against the −0.026 excess-of-cash headline
it would have looked like a *larger* adverse effect out of sample; it is in fact a
fractionally smaller one. Neither reading is close to |*t*| = 2.)

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

| World | bands − annual Sharpe diff | HAC *t* >= 2 |
|---|--:|--:|
| Planted: dispersion mean-reverts (60-day half-life) | **+0.041** (sd 0.009) | **7 / 8 seeds** |
| Null: dispersion is a random walk | +0.004 (sd 0.014) | **0 / 8 seeds** |

On a world built to reward acting on dispersion, the band rule beats the calendar rule
cleanly and repeatably; on a world where dispersion never reverts, it does not. The
harness reads the sign correctly, so the flat real-tape result is a fact about SPY/IEF/GLD,
not a broken detector.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** Across two books, two windows, two eras, six cost levels and five
  band widths, **no schedule difference clears |*t*| = 2 in any specification**. The
  headline bands-minus-annual excess Sharpe is **−0.026** (HAC *t* on the return difference
  **+0.82**), with a paired block-bootstrap CI of **[−0.067, +0.014]** that straddles zero;
  the 3-asset book gives −0.028 (*t* = +0.80) and the 23-year SPY/IEF cross-check −0.032
  gross-of-cash (*t* = +1.04) against a −0.034 gross-of-cash comparator on the headline
  window. Daryanani's reported ~0.5 pp/yr advantage for opportunistic bands over
  annual rebalancing does **not** reproduce here: the measured CAGR gap is **+0.09 pp/yr**,
  a fifth of the claim and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The intervals are
  tight, so this is a precise null rather than a weak test.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is nothing to bank. Turnover under every schedule is
  7–17% of NAV a year, so even a 50 bps one-way cost — ten times realistic — separates the
  schedules by **under 4 basis points of annual drag**. Choosing bands over the calendar
  changes the risk-adjusted outcome by roughly the width of the bid-ask spread. The only
  first-order cost this study does **not** model is **tax**, which runs against the
  higher-turnover schedules and would make the quarterly book strictly worse in a taxable
  account, not better.
- **What is real.** Rebalancing on *some* schedule is genuine **risk control**: the
  do-nothing book ended the sample at 84.6% equity, a portfolio nobody chose. Among the
  schedules that do control risk, the 5/25 band rule gives the tightest weight envelope
  (53.6–65.2% equity) for 27% less traded notional than quarterly — though annual is
  cheaper still (with a far wider envelope) and quarterly tracks target more closely *on
  average*. That — not a Sharpe edge — is the honest case for tolerance bands, and it is a
  case about *governance*, not about return.
